# Summary

*Frankenstein; or, the Modern Prometheus* by Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley is a classic novel made freely available through Project Gutenberg (eBook #84, first released October 1, 1993, and most recently updated February 10, 2026). The text is distributed at no cost under the Project Gutenberg License and can be freely copied, shared, and reused, with minimal restrictions for users in the United States and most other countries. The eBook is available in English and multiple formats on www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/84, with credits to several editors and digital formatters who prepared this version for public access.

# Summary

In a letter dated December 11th from St. Petersburgh to his sister Margaret, Robert Walton assures her that his ambitious Arctic expedition has commenced successfully and expresses his growing confidence. Having arrived safely, he describes feeling invigorated by the northern cold and envisions discovering a passage near the pole, unlocking the secrets of magnetism, and exploring unprecedented lands of eternal light. Walton's passion stems from a lifelong fascination with polar voyages sparked by his uncle's library, though he briefly pursued poetry before inheriting a cousin's fortune, which redirected him toward exploration. Over six years, he disciplined himself through whale-fishing expeditions and studies in mathematics and science to prepare for this voyage. Despite his firm resolve, he acknowledges fluctuating hopes and the emotional burden of leadership. He plans to depart for Archangel within three weeks, hire a ship, and set sail in June, uncertain when—or if—he will return, asking Margaret for her blessings as he embarks on this perilous yet purposeful endeavor.

# Summary

Robert Walton writes to his sister Margaret from Archangel on March 28th, describing his preparations for an Arctic maritime expedition. He has hired a vessel and engaged trustworthy sailors, but laments his profound loneliness and lack of an intellectually compatible friend to share his ambitions and counsel his impulsive nature. Though self-educated and feeling inadequately learned, he expresses unwavering determination to proceed with his voyage once weather permits. He praises his lieutenant's courage and enterprise, and particularly commends his master—a man of exceptional gentleness and integrity whose noble sacrifice of his own happiness for a young Russian woman's sake demonstrates uncommon virtue despite his lack of education. Walton acknowledges that his passionate enthusiasm for oceanic exploration stems partly from his imaginative nature and romantic reading, yet assures Margaret of his prudence. He closes by asking her to continue writing, as her letters may sustain him during the arduous journey ahead.

# Summary

In this letter dated July 7th, Captain R.W. writes to his sister Mrs. Saville from an Arctic voyage to assure her of his safety and good progress. Though he may not return to England for years, he reports high morale among his crew despite the dangers of floating ice in these northern latitudes. He has encountered only minor incidents—a few gales and a small leak—and remains in good spirits, bolstered by unexpected warm southern winds. R.W. pledges to be prudent and avoid rash dangers while expressing unwavering confidence that his determined will and perseverance will ultimately lead to success in his endeavor, as the stars themselves seem to witness his triumph.

# Summary

On August 5th, Captain Walton writes to Mrs. Saville describing a remarkable incident during his Arctic expedition. While trapped in ice near the North Pole, Walton's crew observes a giant figure traveling by dog sledge across the frozen wasteland. The following morning, they rescue an emaciated European man drifting on an ice fragment—apparently pursuing the giant figure he calls a "daemon." The stranger, initially taciturn and grief-stricken, gradually recovers and forms a deep bond with Walton. When Walton expresses his willingness to sacrifice everything for knowledge and exploration, the stranger is visibly disturbed and cryptically warns him against such ambitions, comparing them to an "intoxicating draught." By August 19th, the stranger agrees to reveal his tragic history, cautioning that his tale of "unparalleled misfortunes" contains a moral lesson about the dangers of pursuing knowledge. Walton pledges to record the stranger's narrative, convinced that his extraordinary story will provide profound insight into the consequences of unchecked ambition.

# Summary

The narrator, a Genevese of distinguished family, recounts how his father—a respected public servant—befriended a merchant named Beaufort who had fallen into poverty and retreated to Lucerne in shame. After ten months of searching, the narrator's father found Beaufort dying of grief, attended by his courageous daughter Caroline, who had sustained them through plain work. Following Beaufort's death, the narrator's father married Caroline two years later, and they traveled through Italy, Germany, and France for her recovery. The narrator was born in Naples and became their cherished only child. When he was five, during a visit to Lake Como, his mother discovered a fair-haired orphan girl—Elizabeth Lavenza, daughter of a Milanese nobleman—living in poverty with peasants. The narrator's parents adopted Elizabeth, and she became the narrator's beloved companion, whom he regarded as his to love and protect forever.

# Summary

Victor Frankenstein recounts his idyllic Swiss childhood spent with his beloved cousin Elizabeth and friend Henry Clerval, whose companionship profoundly shaped his character. While Elizabeth found joy in nature's beauty and Clerval pursued heroic adventures and moral endeavors, Victor became consumed by an intense, insatiable curiosity about nature's secrets. At age thirteen, he discovered occult texts by Cornelius Agrippa, which his father dismissively rejected—a pivotal moment that deepened Victor's obsession with alchemy, the philosopher's stone, and raising the dead rather than steering him toward legitimate science. This misguided passion dominated him until age fifteen, when witnessing a lightning strike destroy an oak tree and a scholar's explanation of electricity and galvanism finally shattered his faith in ancient mysticism. Victor then turned to mathematics, believing this shift saved him from ruin. However, he recognizes in retrospect that this apparent salvation was illusory; destiny had already set him on the path to his eventual destruction, for his fundamental thirst for forbidden knowledge remained undiminished and would ultimately drive him toward catastrophe.

# Summary

At seventeen, the narrator leaves Geneva to study at the University of Ingolstadt, but tragedy strikes first when his beloved mother dies after nursing his cousin Elizabeth through scarlet fever. Though grief-stricken, he eventually departs for university, where he meets two professors of natural philosophy: the dismissive M. Krempe, who ridicules his previous studies of alchemy, and the kind, inspiring M. Waldman, whose lecture on modern chemistry's miraculous achievements profoundly moves him. Waldman's endorsement of chemistry and encouragement transform the narrator's academic direction, igniting an obsessive ambition to explore nature's deepest mysteries and achieve unprecedented scientific breakthroughs—a fateful decision that will determine his future.

# Summary

The narrator becomes intensely devoted to natural philosophy and chemistry, studying under professors Krempe and Waldman at the University of Ingolstadt. His passionate pursuit of knowledge leads him to investigate the mysteries of life and death, ultimately discovering the secret to animating lifeless matter. Driven by obsessive ambition and fueled by the belief that he can create life itself, he constructs an eight-foot-tall human creature from collected body parts in a secluded workshop. Throughout months of grueling labor during the summer and fall, his dedication consumes him entirely—he neglects his family, neglects nature's beauty, and his health deteriorates as he works ceaselessly toward completing his creation. Though warned by his own experience about the dangers of unchecked intellectual pursuit, he refuses to divulge his discovery, cautioning his listener that the acquisition of such knowledge brings misery rather than happiness. The narrator concludes by acknowledging that his singular obsession has destroyed his peace of mind and relationships, reducing him to a diseased and anxious state.

# Summary

On a dreary November night in Ingolstadt, Victor Frankenstein completes his two-year obsession of creating life and witnesses his creature awakening with horror and revulsion. The being's grotesque appearance—with yellow skin, watery eyes, and shriveled complexion—devastates Frankenstein, who had envisioned beauty. After a sleepless night tormented by nightmares and a terrifying encounter with the monster in his bedroom, Frankenstein flees into the streets in psychological anguish. He is rescued from despair by the unexpected arrival of his childhood friend Henry Clerval, whose presence temporarily restores his composure. However, Frankenstein's relief at finding his apartment empty of the creature is followed by a complete mental and physical collapse—a nervous fever lasting several months. Throughout his recovery, Henry serves as his devoted nurse while Frankenstein raves deliriously about the monster. With the arrival of spring and Henry's steadfast care, Frankenstein gradually regains his health and spirits, though the image of his created creature remains permanently haunting.

# Summary

Elizabeth Lavenza writes to her cousin Victor to express concern about his illness in Ingolstadt and urge his recovery and return home. She updates him on family matters, including his father's vigorous health, his younger brother Ernest's desire for military service, and the return of Justine Moritz—a beloved family servant who had been taken in as a child and later left to care for her repentant but troubled mother. Elizabeth also mentions young William and provides Geneva gossip about local marriages. Victor, moved by the letter, begins to recover and eventually leaves his sickbed. However, he experiences severe distress when professors praise his scientific work, as he harbors traumatic memories of his natural philosophy studies. With Clerval's compassionate support, Victor redirects his studies toward Oriental languages and takes a restorative walking tour through the countryside, during which his spirits and health are fully restored, allowing him to feel genuine happiness once more.

# Summary

Victor Frankenstein receives a devastating letter from his father informing him that his younger brother William has been murdered in Geneva. The family discovered William's lifeless body on the morning of May 7th, bearing the marks of strangulation on his neck. A valuable miniature of Victor's mother, which William had borrowed from Elizabeth, was found in the pocket of Justine Moritz, a beloved family servant, leading to her arrest as the suspected murderer. Distraught, Victor rushes home to Geneva, and during a stormy night near Plainpalais where William died, he glimpses his creature—the monster he created—fleeing across Mont Salêve. Convinced that his creation is responsible for William's death, Victor is tormented by guilt yet remains silent, fearing no one would believe his extraordinary tale. Upon arriving home, he finds his family devastated and learns that Justine is to be tried that day, though both Victor and Elizabeth are certain of her innocence. Victor resolves to prove Justine's acquittal but is paralyzed by the knowledge that his own created monster is the true murderer.

# Summary

At Justine Moritz's trial for the murder of Victor Frankenstein's brother William, Victor suffers anguish knowing her innocence while unable to reveal the true killer—the creature he created. Despite Justine's calm demeanor and convincing defense, damning circumstantial evidence—including William's portrait found in her pocket—turns public opinion against her. Elizabeth passionately testifies to Justine's character, but character witnesses prove timid. The jury condemns Justine unanimously, and though she initially confesses under pressure from her confessor threatening excommunication, she later reveals to Elizabeth and Victor that she lied to obtain absolution. Unable to convince the judges of his suspicions without appearing mad, Victor watches helplessly as Justine is executed. Devastated by guilt, Victor recognizes that his creation of the monster has destroyed not only William but also innocent Justine, and he despairs over the suffering he has inflicted upon his family.

# Summary

Victor Frankenstein, tormented by remorse and guilt following Justine's death—a victim of the monster he created—suffers intense psychological anguish that devastates his health and relationships. Though his father urges him to find strength and his beloved Elizabeth offers comfort and love, Victor remains trapped in despair, haunted by fear that the creature will commit further murders and consumed by murderous rage toward his creation. Seeking relief from his unbearable emotional torment, Victor abandons his home and journeys to the Alpine valley of Chamounix in August, nearly two months after Justine's death. During this solitary expedition through magnificent mountain landscapes—including Mont Blanc and vast glaciers—Victor experiences fleeting moments of peace and natural beauty that temporarily soothe his anguish, though grief and terror repeatedly overwhelm him, ultimately granting him only brief respite and fitful sleep upon arrival at Chamounix village.

# Summary

The narrator, seeking solace in nature, spends a day in the Alpine valley observing the Arveiron glacier and surrounding mountains. Though initially comforted by the sublime landscape, his melancholy returns with the next morning's rain. Determined to recapture the spiritual uplift he had previously experienced, he ascends Montanvert alone despite the treacherous, desolate path. Upon reaching the glacier's edge, overcome with emotion, he suddenly encounters the hideous creature he had created advancing toward him across the ice at superhuman speed. Despite his initial rage and desire for combat, the creature pleads with Frankenstein to hear his tale, arguing that as his creator, Frankenstein owes him compassion and happiness. The creature threatens to destroy Frankenstein's remaining loved ones if denied. Though torn by hatred and revulsion, Frankenstein is moved by the creature's arguments about creator's duties and his own curiosity about his brother's murder, and reluctantly agrees to listen to the creature's story in a nearby mountain hut.

# Summary

This passage depicts the creature's awakening and early experiences from Mary Shelley's *Frankenstein*. The creature emerges confused and overwhelmed by sensations, gradually learning to distinguish between sight, sound, smell, and touch. After wandering from Ingolstadt forest, he discovers fire, learns to cook food, and eventually finds shelter near a cottage. Terrified by villagers who attack him, he takes refuge in a hovel adjoining a small cottage. Through a crevice, he observes a family—an elderly man, a young woman, and a young man—living in poverty but with great kindness and affection toward one another. Fascinated by their gentle interactions, musical instrument playing, and domestic routines, the creature experiences complex emotions of pleasure and pain for the first time, beginning his long observation of human society and his longing to connect with humanity.

# Summary

The narrator, a solitary creature living in a hovel, observes a poor cottager family consisting of a blind old man (father), his son Felix, and daughter Agatha. Initially afraid to approach them after suffering mistreatment from villagers, the narrator instead watches them closely, admiring their gentle manners, mutual affection, and kindness despite their poverty and hunger. Moved by their suffering, the narrator secretly assists them by gathering firewood at night and foraging for his own food instead of stealing theirs. Over months, the narrator learns their language by listening intently, mastering words like "fire," "bread," and their names. However, upon seeing his own monstrous reflection in a pool, the narrator becomes despondent about his hideous appearance. Despite this, he continues observing the family, performing invisible acts of kindness, and fantasizing about eventually revealing himself and gaining their love through gentle demeanor and linguistic ability. As spring arrives and the family's circumstances improve, the narrator's spirits lift with hope for a better future and the possibility of acceptance.

# Summary

As spring transforms the desolate landscape into blooming beauty, the narrator observes the cottage inhabitants with growing fascination. When Safie, a beautiful Arabian woman, arrives on horseback, she brings joy to the melancholy household, particularly to Felix, who greets her with rapture. Though Safie speaks a different language, she begins learning with the family, and the narrator, hidden from view, simultaneously acquires their language and knowledge through observation. As Safie receives instruction from Felix using Volney's *Ruins of Empires*, the narrator gains profound insights into human history, society, virtue, and vice. However, this education becomes torturous as he learns about property, rank, and family bonds—realizing he possesses none of these and is a hideous creature utterly unlike humanity. The accumulation of knowledge intensifies his anguish and alienation, leaving him to contemplate whether he is a monster doomed to isolation, even as he deeply loves and reveres his unknowing protectors.

# Summary

The narrator learns the history of the De Lacey family, a French aristocratic household fallen into ruin. De Lacey's son Felix attempted to rescue a Turkish merchant imprisoned in Paris on charges the narrator believes were unjust, motivated partly by the merchant's beautiful daughter, Safie. Felix facilitated the merchant's escape, but the French government discovered the plot and imprisoned De Lacey and his daughter Agatha, stripping them of their fortune and exiling them. Felix surrendered himself hoping to free them but failed. The Turkish merchant, ungrateful for his rescue and disapproving of Safie's attachment to the Christian Felix, abandoned them with only a pittance. Safie, however, rejected her father's command to return to Turkey, chose Christianity and independence over harem life, and traveled alone to Germany to reunite with Felix at his family's impoverished cottage, arriving safely with assistance from strangers.

# Summary

The creature recounts how three foundational books—*Paradise Lost*, *Plutarch's Lives*, and *The Sorrows of Werter*—profoundly shaped his intellectual and emotional development after he discovered them in a leather portmanteau. While *Plutarch* inspired admiration for virtue and heroic figures, and *Werter* evoked despair through its melancholic reflections, *Paradise Lost* struck deepest, as he identified with both Adam's isolation and Satan's envious anguish at witnessing others' happiness. The creature's despair intensified when he found Victor's laboratory journal, which documented his own horrifying creation in brutal detail, yet he remained hopeful that the cottagers' virtue and benevolence would overcome their prejudice against his hideous appearance. After months of preparation and observation—during which the cottage's happiness increased with Safie's arrival—the creature resolved to approach the blind old man, De Lacey, alone, believing his voice might win compassion without the horror of his appearance. # Summary

In this passage from *Frankenstein*, the creature recounts his descent into murderous rage and despair following his rejection by the De Lacey family. After frightening them and causing them to abandon their cottage, he burns it down in vengeance. He then travels to Geneva to confront his creator, Victor Frankenstein, seeking justice. During his journey, he saves a drowning girl but is shot by a man who mistakes him for a threat, further confirming his belief that humanity will never accept him. Upon reaching Geneva, the creature encounters Victor's young son William and, learning the boy's identity, murders him in an act of revenge against his creator. He plants a portrait of a beautiful woman on a sleeping girl to frame her for the crime. Consumed by loneliness and bitterness, the creature demands that Victor create a female companion for him—a being as hideous as himself—threatening that they will not part until Victor agrees to this demand.

# Summary

In this passage from *Frankenstein*, Victor's creature demands that Victor create a female companion, arguing that his malice stems from misery and rejection by humanity. The creature appeals to Victor's sense of justice, promising to exile himself to South America with his companion and live peacefully away from mankind. Though initially horrified and refusing, Victor becomes moved by the creature's eloquent arguments and threats, eventually consenting to the demand in exchange for the creature's oath to leave Europe forever. After the creature departs, Victor descends the mountain in emotional turmoil, tormented by doubt and dread about the consequences of his promise. He returns to Geneva deeply disturbed, resolving to fulfill his obligation despite his inner anguish and foreboding.

# Summary

Victor Frankenstein returns to Geneva unable to commence creating a female companion for his creature, fearing both the monster's vengeance and his own repugnance for the task. Though his health improves and spirits lift during solitary lake retreats, his melancholy periodically returns. When his father observes Victor's recovery, he suggests an immediate marriage to their cousin Elizabeth, whom Victor has loved since childhood. Victor expresses genuine affection for Elizabeth but cannot marry until fulfilling his promise to the creature. Resolving to travel to England to conduct necessary research in solitude, Victor conceals his true motives while obtaining his father's consent. His friend Clerval is arranged as his companion, departing in late September. During their journey down the Rhine to Rotterdam and across the sea, Victor remains tormented by dark thoughts while Clerval delights in the landscape's beauty. Though Victor briefly finds peace observing the scenery, he remains enslaved to his grim purpose. They arrive in England in late December, with Victor's sole focus on completing his detested task before claiming Elizabeth as his reward.

# Summary

The narrator and his friend Clerval spend several months in London, where the narrator uses letters of introduction to meet distinguished natural philosophers in pursuit of information to fulfill a dark promise. Though tormented by guilt over the deaths of William and Justine, the narrator attempts to conceal his anguish from the cheerful Clerval, who is eager to gain knowledge and experience. After four months, they leave London on March 27th and travel northward through England and Scotland—visiting Windsor, Oxford, Matlock, and the Lake District—eventually arriving in Perth. The journey offers the narrator temporary solace in nature but is overshadowed by his dread that the creature he created will seek vengeance on his loved ones if he delays. Upon reaching Perth, the narrator separates from Clerval and travels to a remote hut on one of the Orkney Islands to complete his gruesome work in solitude, driven by an anxious hope tinged with dark forebodings.

# Summary

Victor Frankenstein, laboring in his laboratory on a moonlit night, experiences a moral awakening regarding his promise to create a female companion for his creature. Horrified by the potential consequences—including the birth of a race of demons that could threaten humanity—he destroys the half-finished creation. The enraged monster appears at his window and, after a confrontation, vows to be present on Victor's wedding night. Victor flees to a remote island, receives a letter from his friend Clerval urging him to join him, and disposes of the remaining remains of his work by casting them into the sea. During his boat journey, Victor is blown off course by a violent storm and eventually reaches an Irish coastal town, where he is arrested on suspicion of murdering a gentleman found dead the previous night, setting in motion a new tragedy.

# Summary

The narrator is brought before magistrate Kirwin to answer charges in the murder of a young man found strangled on an Irish shore. Witnesses testify that fishermen discovered the body, which bore fingermarks on the neck, and that a boat matching the narrator's had been seen leaving the area. When the narrator is taken to view the corpse, he is horrified to discover it is his beloved friend Henry Clerval, and he collapses in convulsions. He falls into a severe fever lasting two months, during which he deliriously confesses to murdering Clerval, William, and Justine. Upon recovering in prison, he is visited by his father, whose arrival brings him comfort. The grand jury eventually rejects the murder charge after evidence proves the narrator was on the Orkney Islands when Clerval's body was found. Freed but profoundly traumatized, the narrator remains consumed by guilt and despair, haunted by Clerval's death and driven by a duty to pursue and destroy the monster he created. He sets sail with his father for Geneva, tormented by nightmares and dependent on laudanum for sleep.

# Summary

After arriving in Paris following a voyage, Victor Frankenstein, emotionally devastated and physically weakened, struggles with the knowledge that he has caused the deaths of Justine, William, and Henry through his creation of a monster. Though his father attempts to help him recover, Victor cannot confide in him about the true source of his suffering. Elizabeth writes to Victor asking whether he loves another, offering him the freedom to choose his own happiness and assuring him she will accept whatever brings him peace. Victor responds affectionately and agrees to marry Elizabeth, but is tormented by the monster's threat to appear on their wedding night. Despite harboring secret dread, Victor proceeds with the wedding plans, telling himself that his death is inevitable anyway. As Victor and Elizabeth depart for Lake Como after their ceremony, traveling by boat toward Evian, Victor is consumed by anxiety about the monster's impending revenge, while Elizabeth senses something ominous despite the beauty of their surroundings.

# Summary

After landing at eight o'clock on the shore of a lake, Victor Frankenstein experiences mounting dread as darkness falls and a violent storm erupts. Armed with a pistol and expecting an attack, he forces his bride Elizabeth to retire to their room while he searches the house. He discovers her murdered body with marks of strangulation around her neck—the work of his creature, whom he glimpses fleeing through the window and shoots at before the monster escapes into the lake. Victor's father dies from shock upon hearing of Elizabeth's death, and Victor himself is institutionalized, deemed mad. Upon his release, consumed by revenge, Victor seeks out a magistrate to report the creature's crimes, but the official finds his account too fantastical to act upon. Frustrated by the magistrate's disbelief and refusal to pursue justice, Victor resolves to hunt down and destroy his creation himself, declaring revenge his sole remaining passion and purpose.

# Combined Summary

In the novel's conclusion, Victor Frankenstein pursues his creature across desolate landscapes from Geneva to the Arctic, driven by revenge for the deaths of his loved ones. Rescued by Captain Walton's ship, the dying Victor urges the captain to continue his vengeful mission, warning that the creature is eloquent and treacherous. When the crew faces mutiny due to being trapped in Arctic ice, Walton initially considers continuing despite their fears. However, when the ice breaks and passage south becomes possible, the sailors demand to turn back. Though Victor refuses to abandon his pursuit, Walton ultimately concedes to his crew's demands and turns toward England. Victor dies shortly after, expressing ambivalence about his destructive quest. That night, Walton discovers the creature mourning over Frankenstein's corpse, wracked with remorse and eloquently expressing his internal torment and capacity for love.
